subtype: Training or class culture as a young teacher [Actor]
passage: On the first morning of induction at the call centre, twenty trainees looked at Bhupen, the twenty-five-year-old trainer, waiting to see what kind of person he would be. Eshaan answered the first question wrongly. Bhupen said, “That's the exact trap I fell into too. Who can say why it's a trap?” Eshaan sat back, relieved. Ten minutes later an older trainee cut in: “That's not how we did it at my last company.” “Note it down,” Bhupen said evenly. “I'll come back to it after the break, and I will.” At the back, a woman who had not spoken yet wrote something down. At the break, a canteen friend asked for the answer sheet early. “Same as everyone, after the test,” Bhupen said, and smiled anyway.

qa.q: How many trainees looked at Bhupen on the first morning?
What might Eshaan have been feeling when Eshaan sat back after Bhupen's answer?
qa.a: Eshaan probably felt relieved, since the wrong answer was met with “That's the exact trap I fell into too” and not with blame.

qa.q: What could Bhupen do next if the older trainee keeps interrupting?
qa.a: Bhupen could keep to the same rule for every interruption, return to the point after the break as promised and, if it continues, speak privately with the trainee.

qa.q: How might the canteen friend have felt about Bhupen's answer?
qa.a: The friend may have felt a little let down, since even a friend got “Same as everyone, after the test,” which shows fairness matters more than being liked.

grounding: A young trainer sets the room's tone by responding calmly to the first mistake and interruption and treating a friend the same as everyone.

subtype: Training or class culture as a young teacher [Actor]
passage:
“Ma'am, ma'am, I know this one—” Noor blurted, half out of the seat, on Nandini's second day as a Class 8 teacher.
“Noor, I'm glad you know. Hand up, please, and I'll come to you next.” Noor sat down, red-faced, hand raised.
“Ma'am, yesterday you let Rohan shout out,” said a boy at the back.
Nandini paused. “You're right. That was unfair to you. From now on the rule is the same for everyone, including me.” A few children grinned. In the corner, Aditi, who had not spoken all week, lifted her hand halfway.
Nandini went to her first. “Yes, Aditi?”
“I didn't get the last step.”
“Thank you. Who else didn't?” Eight hands went up.

qa.q: On which day of Nandini's teaching did Noor blurt out the answer?
qa.a: It was Nandini's second day as a Class 8 teacher.

qa.q: How did Nandini likely feel when the boy said she had let Rohan shout out?
qa.a: She likely felt caught out and a little embarrassed, pausing before admitting the slip rather than protecting her image as the teacher.

qa.q: What did Nandini's handling of the first interruption teach the class?
qa.a: It taught that a hand up gets you a turn, that the rule is the same for everyone, and that saying you did not understand is welcome.

qa.q: How might Aditi have felt when Nandini went to her first?
qa.a: Aditi probably felt surprised and brave, since it was the first time Aditi had spoken all week, and safer when eight hands went up.

grounding: A young teacher sets the room's tone with her first response to an interruption, applying the same rule to all.
